original_question: Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble.
target_in_paper: Problem 21.31 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)": "Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble."
correct_elements: Your draft matches the target problem in the paper essentially verbatim. It has the correct hypothesis on N (finite and soluble), the correct ambient object (the holomorph Hol(N) of N), the correct class of subgroups (regular subgroups), and the correct conclusion (they should also be soluble).
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, the quantified subgroup should be named explicitly: for every subgroup R <= Hol(N) that is regular on the underlying set N, is R soluble?
The paper's nearby definition of holomorph should be unpacked: Hol(N) is the normalizer in the full permutation group Sym(N) of the subgroup of left translations of N.
The term "regular subgroup" should be defined explicitly for self-containment: it means a subgroup of Sym(N) acting sharply transitively on N.
There are no additional hypotheses, exceptions, or paper-internal equivalent reformulations attached to Problem 21.31 in this source.
refined_question: Let N be a finite soluble group. Viewing N as a set, let Hol(N) denote the normalizer in Sym(N) of the subgroup of left translations of N. Must every subgroup R <= Hol(N) that acts regularly on N be a soluble group?
justification: The supplied arXiv source is the Kourovka Notebook rather than a conventional article with a numbered introduction and statements such as Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, and Theorem 1.3. In this source, your draft is already the exact target statement: Problem 21.31. The only refinement needed is to spell out the standard meanings of Hol(N) and of a regular subgroup so that the question is self-contained. The notebook does give a definition of holomorph elsewhere, in 20.108, but it does not provide an equivalent reformulation of 21.31.
